findings.title: NoSQL ($where) JavaScript injection via allocations threshold parameter
findings.attack_path: Authenticated user requests GET /allocations/<id>?threshold=<payload>. getByUserIdAndThreshold interpolates the raw threshold into a MongoDB $where clause: {$where: `this.userId == ${parsedUserId} && this.stocks > '${threshold}'`}. The threshold is never parsed or escaped (the parseInt fix is commented out), so payloads like 0';while(true){} or 1'; return 1=='1 execute arbitrary server-side JavaScript inside the database engine, enabling data exfiltration of all documents and a denial-of-service infinite loop.
findings.remediation: Uncomment the parseInt(threshold,10) validation, reject values outside 0-99, and never build $where from user input. Prefer a typed comparison query ({stocks: {$gt: n}}) and disable server-side JavaScript execution in MongoDB.

findings.title: Server-side JavaScript injection through eval() of contribution inputs
findings.attack_path: An authenticated user POSTs to /contributions with preTax/afterTax/roth fields. handleContributionsUpdate calls eval(req.body.preTax) (and the other two) directly on the request body before validation. A payload such as global.process.mainModule.require('child_process').execSync('id') runs arbitrary Node.js code in the application process, giving full remote code execution.
findings.remediation: Replace all eval() calls with parseInt(req.body.field, 10) (the commented fix) and validate numeric ranges. Never pass user-controlled strings to eval/Function.

findings.title: User passwords stored and compared in plaintext
findings.attack_path: UserDAO.addUser writes the raw password field to the users collection (the bcrypt.hashSync fix is commented out) and validateLogin compares with strict string equality. Any read access to MongoDB (via TM-001, a backup, or a misconfigured instance) exposes every credential in cleartext, enabling immediate account takeover and credential reuse against other systems.
findings.remediation: Hash passwords with bcrypt (genSalt + hashSync) on signup and use bcrypt.compareSync on login. Migrate existing plaintext credentials and force resets.

findings.title: Stored XSS via shared memos rendered with disabled autoescape and ineffective marked sanitize
findings.attack_path: POST /memos stores req.body.memo verbatim in a shared memos collection read by every user. displayMemos renders {{ marked(doc.memo) }} while swig autoescape is globally disabled (swig.setDefaults autoescape:false) and marked 0.3.5's sanitize option is deprecated/bypassable. A low-privileged attacker stores a script payload; when an administrator opens /memos the script executes in the admin session, stealing the (non-httpOnly) session cookie and escalating to full account/admin takeover.
findings.remediation: Re-enable swig autoescape, stop trusting marked's sanitize flag (use DOMPurify on rendered HTML), set httpOnly session cookies, and scope memos per user instead of one shared collection.

findings.title: Missing function-level authorization on /benefits admin endpoint
findings.attack_path: Routes register GET/POST /benefits with only isLoggedIn; the isAdmin guard is commented out. Any authenticated non-admin user can call POST /benefits to modify other users' benefitStartDate and enumerate all non-admin users, exercising an admin-only business function (vertical privilege escalation).
findings.remediation: Add the isAdmin middleware to both /benefits routes (the commented fix) and enforce server-side role checks on every privileged action.

findings.title: IDOR on /allocations/:userId exposes other users' financial data
findings.attack_path: displayAllocations reads userId from req.params instead of req.session (the session-based fix is commented out). An authenticated user iterates the numeric userId path segment to read any other user's allocation records and identity fields (userName, firstName, lastName) returned by the join, a horizontal authorization bypass over an enumerable integer key.
findings.remediation: Derive userId from req.session, not the URL, or enforce an ownership check that the requested userId matches the authenticated principal.

findings.title: Server-Side Request Forgery via /research url/symbol parameters
findings.attack_path: displayResearch builds url = req.query.url + req.query.symbol and passes it straight to needle.get, writing the response body back to the client. An authenticated attacker sets url to an internal address (e.g. http://169.254.169.254/ metadata, http://localhost:27017, or internal admin services) to read internal-only resources and pivot, with the response reflected verbatim.
findings.remediation: Remove the user-supplied url entirely; pin the upstream data provider host server-side, allowlist schemes/hosts, and block link-local/private/loopback ranges.

findings.title: Hardcoded application secrets and committed TLS private key
findings.attack_path: config/env/all.js hardcodes cookieSecret ('session_cookie_secret_key_here') and cryptoKey/cryptoAlgo, and artifacts/cert/server.key (a real RSA PRIVATE KEY) plus server.crt are committed to the repo. Anyone with repo access can forge/tamper session cookies signed with the known secret and impersonate the TLS endpoint, undermining session integrity and confidentiality.
findings.remediation: Move all secrets to environment variables/secret manager, generate per-deployment random values, rotate the leaked key/cert, and remove them from version control history.

findings.title: Default seeded accounts with weak, predictable credentials
findings.attack_path: artifacts/db-reset.js seeds an admin account (userName 'admin', password 'Admin_123', isAdmin:true) and predictable users user1/user2 with passwords User1_123/User2_123. These are committed in source and stored in plaintext (TM-003), so an attacker logs in directly as administrator using the published credentials, immediately gaining full privileged access.
findings.remediation: Do not seed real/default admin credentials in any non-throwaway environment; require an interactive admin bootstrap with a forced strong password change, and hash all seeded passwords.

findings.title: Reflected/stored XSS via profile fields with autoescape disabled and wrong-context encoding
findings.attack_path: Profile fields (firstName, lastName, ssn, dob, address, bankAcc) are stored and rendered into profile.html with swig autoescape globally off. The website value is HTML-encoded with ESAPI but then placed into an href URL context (and firstNameSafeString into href), the wrong encoding context, allowing javascript:-scheme and attribute-breakout payloads to execute script in the victim's session.
findings.remediation: Enable swig autoescape, apply context-correct encoding (encodeForURL for href targets), and validate/normalize URL fields to http(s) schemes only.

findings.title: Sensitive PII (SSN, DOB, bank account) stored unencrypted at rest
findings.attack_path: ProfileDAO.updateUser writes ssn, dob, bankAcc, bankRouting as plaintext to the users collection (the crypto encrypt/decrypt helpers are commented out). Any database read primitive (TM-001 $where injection, a stolen backup, or direct port-27017 access) yields regulated financial PII in the clear, a reportable data breach.
findings.remediation: Encrypt SSN/DOB/financial fields at the application layer with a managed key (the commented crypto path, fixed to use a per-record IV) and enforce field-level access control and encryption at rest.

findings.title: Application served over plaintext HTTP with no transport encryption
findings.attack_path: server.js starts http.createServer (the https path is commented out) so credentials, session cookies, SSN and bank data all traverse the network in cleartext. A network-positioned attacker (shared Wi-Fi, on-path) captures credentials and session cookies and replays them to take over accounts.
findings.remediation: Terminate TLS (enable the https server or a TLS-terminating proxy), redirect HTTP to HTTPS, and set HSTS via helmet.

findings.title: Insecure session cookie configuration (no httpOnly/secure, saveUninitialized, resave)
findings.attack_path: express-session is configured with saveUninitialized:true and resave:true and no cookie options, so the session cookie lacks httpOnly and secure flags. Combined with the stored XSS (TM-004), document.cookie is readable by injected script; over HTTP (TM-012) the cookie is also sniffable, enabling session hijacking.
findings.remediation: Set cookie {httpOnly:true, secure:true, sameSite:'lax', maxAge}, use saveUninitialized:false, a generic cookie name, and a persistent server-side session store.

findings.title: Open redirect via /learn url parameter
findings.attack_path: GET /learn does res.redirect(req.query.url) with no validation. An attacker crafts /learn?url=https://evil.example to send a victim from a trusted origin to a phishing/credential-harvesting page, lending legitimacy to the lure.
findings.remediation: Allowlist redirect targets or restrict to relative same-origin paths; reject absolute external URLs.

findings.title: No CSRF protection on state-changing POST endpoints
findings.attack_path: csurf is imported but commented out, so POST /profile, /contributions, /benefits and /memos accept cross-site requests with the ambient session cookie (no SameSite either, TM-013). A victim who visits an attacker page is silently forced to change profile PII, submit contributions, or (for an admin) modify benefits.
findings.remediation: Enable csurf (or equivalent), emit and validate per-session CSRF tokens on all state-changing routes, and set SameSite on the session cookie.

findings.title: Regular Expression Denial of Service in profile bankRouting validation
findings.attack_path: handleProfileUpdate validates bankRouting with /([0-9]+)+#/ — nested quantifiers that backtrack catastrophically. An authenticated user submits a long digit string with no trailing # (e.g. 30+ digits) on POST /profile, pinning a CPU core and blocking the single-threaded event loop, degrading availability for all users.
findings.remediation: Replace with the linear pattern /([0-9]+)#/ and add input length limits; consider a non-backtracking validator.

findings.title: Verbose error handler discloses stack traces to clients
findings.attack_path: The error middleware renders the full error object (error-template.html) to the response with status 500. Triggering an unhandled error returns internal stack traces, file paths and library versions, aiding reconnaissance and exploit targeting.
findings.remediation: Return a generic error page to clients, log details server-side only, and disable detailed error rendering in production.

findings.title: Vulnerable and outdated dependencies (marked, mongodb driver, swig, base image)
findings.attack_path: package.json pins known-old components: marked 0.3.5 (ReDoS/XSS-prone), swig 1.4.2 (unmaintained), mongodb ^2.x (legacy $where), and the Dockerfile uses node:12-alpine (EOL runtime). An attacker exploits a published CVE in any of these to achieve XSS, DoS, or injection without needing a novel bug.
findings.remediation: Upgrade to maintained versions, run automated SCA (npm audit / retire.js in CI), and rebuild on a supported Node LTS base image.

findings.title: Log injection / log forging via unencoded username on failed login
findings.attack_path: handleLoginRequest logs the raw userName on a failed login (console.log('...invalid user: ', userName)) with no CRLF encoding (the ESAPI fix is commented out). An unauthenticated attacker submits a username containing newlines to inject forged log lines, corrupting audit trails and confusing downstream log processors.
findings.remediation: Strip/encode CR/LF before logging (e.g. userName.replace(/(\r\n|\r|\n)/g,'_') or ESAPI encodeForHTML/JavaScript) and log via structured logging.

findings.title: Missing security response headers (no helmet: clickjacking, MIME sniffing, no CSP)
findings.attack_path: helmet and dont-sniff-mimetype are imported but commented out and x-powered-by is left enabled. With no X-Frame-Options/CSP the app can be framed for clickjacking, no X-Content-Type-Options allows MIME sniffing, and no CSP weakens XSS defense-in-depth (compounding TM-004/TM-010).
findings.remediation: Enable helmet with frameguard, noSniff, a restrictive CSP and HSTS, and disable x-powered-by.

findings.title: Username enumeration via distinct login error messages
findings.attack_path: handleLoginRequest returns 'Invalid username' versus 'Invalid password' (the unified-error fix is commented out). An attacker probes the login form to distinguish valid accounts, building a target list for credential stuffing/brute force (compounding the weak passwords in TM-022).
findings.remediation: Return one generic 'Invalid username and/or password' message for both cases and apply uniform timing.

findings.title: Weak password policy permits trivial passwords
findings.attack_path: validateSignup enforces only PASS_RE = /^.{1,20}$/ (the complexity fix is commented out), so single-character or dictionary passwords are accepted. Combined with username enumeration (TM-021) and no lockout, accounts fall quickly to brute force / credential stuffing.
findings.remediation: Enforce length>=12 with complexity (the commented strong regex or zxcvbn), add rate limiting and account lockout, and check against breached-password lists.

findings.title: No session regeneration on login enables session fixation
findings.attack_path: handleLoginRequest sets req.session.userId without calling req.session.regenerate (the fix is noted but not applied; only signup regenerates). An attacker who fixes a victim's pre-auth session id (feasible over HTTP / without secure cookie) retains a valid authenticated session after the victim logs in.
findings.remediation: Call req.session.regenerate() on every successful login before assigning userId, and rotate the session id on privilege changes.
